metadata.title: Required number and type of raters in Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) research: domain-specific evidence
metadata.purpose: Structured evidence summary for incorporation into a scientific manuscript.
metadata.scope_note: Based on a time-limited literature search. Absence of a study here does not establish absence from the literature.

instructions_for_manuscript_agent: Cite via the bibkey fields, which match entries in the companion .bib file.
Check verification_level before citing a number. Values 'abstract_or_secondary' and 'excerpts' require checking against the original paper.
All text is paraphrased. No wording here should be presented as a direct quotation; retrieve quotes from the originals.
Do not compare required rater numbers across studies without stating the reliability target and object of measurement.
Fields under author_synthesis and planning_recommendations are interpretations from this review, not published findings. Do not attribute them to the cited authors.
Do not state that Cseh and Jeffries (2019) explicitly require domain-by-domain determination of rater numbers. See cseh_jeffries_2019.framing_caveat.

verification_levels.full_text: Checked against full text or an accepted manuscript.
verification_levels.excerpts: Checked against partial full-text excerpts; some values were not retrieved.
verification_levels.abstract_or_secondary: Known only from an abstract or from citation in another paper.

evidence_classes.a: Directly and empirically tested required rater number or rater load.
evidence_classes.b: Reports reliability for a given panel only.
evidence_classes.c: Recommendation without a dedicated empirical basis.

bottom_line.summary: No domain has a validated, general required number of raters. Published figures are conditional on reliability target, rater expertise and training, scale design, product heterogeneity, number of products and scoring format.

patterns.condition: Trained or expert raters scoring short, homogeneous responses (divergent thinking, captions)
patterns.finding: About 2-5 raters reach relative reliability near .80.

patterns.condition: Novices judging expert-domain products (poems, stories, engineering designs)
patterns.finding: Random panels of 10 novices average alpha of about .53-.66. Very large panels can reach high alpha yet converge poorly with experts (poetry: r = .22).

patterns.condition: Open-ended products rated by non-experts (fashion, design)
patterns.finding: About 7-15 raters for stable aggregate scores; 15-20 for composite indices.

patterns.condition: Person-level measurement with high person-by-task variance
patterns.finding: Adding raters stops helping. With 2 divergent-thinking items, no panel of 1-10 lay raters reached .80 (Hass et al., 2018). More tasks are needed.

patterns.condition: Sport/tactical creativity, music, mathematics, advertising, programming
patterns.finding: No empirical rater-number study located; reliability reports or conventions only.

criticisms.content: Expertise is undefined and domain-dependent. Evidence on experts versus novices is equivocal: expertise increases consensus only sometimes, and when or why it is vital is unclear. Quasi-experts substituted for experts in writing but not engineering (Kaufman et al., 2013). Sufficient type and length of experience remain open.

Amabile (1982) tied the number to achieving acceptable agreement rather than fixing one. Silvia et al. (2008) and Kaufman, Plucker and Baer (2008; 5-10 judges) offer rough guidance. Practice ranges from 2 judges (Daly et al., 2016; 439 engineering designs; agreement .70) to 134 lay judges; Amabile's own studies used 3-21. The authors list the number needed for reliable consensus as an open research question.
More than 10 judges is argued to raise Type I error risk for inter-rater reliability; fewer than 5 is argued to raise both error types. This is conceptual, not empirical.
criticisms.author_synthesis: The analogy arguably conflates a genuine reliability gain from a larger panel mean with a false positive, and does not address whether larger-panel consensus is valid.

criticisms.content: Cronbach's alpha is the default largely by convention. Consistency and absolute agreement are seldom distinguished (citing Stefanic and Randles, 2015), ICC forms are seldom declared, and designs where raters score different subsets are rarely addressed. JRT (Myszkowski and Storme) is noted as a model-based alternative.

Rater fatigue and items per judge (about 3,564 ratings per judge in one reused dataset), scale granularity (3-10 points), training and calibration versus the CAT's theoretical neutrality, and whether some tasks have any appropriate expert.

cseh_jeffries_2019.framing_caveat: Cseh and Jeffries do not explicitly state that rater numbers must be determined separately per domain. That follows from their evidence on domain-by-expertise interactions and from G-theory authors such as van Hooijdonk et al. (2022), who argue that each assessment procedure needs its own G- and D-study.

studies.notes: Gain in dependability diminishes after 3-4 raters. Authors' summary: 2 raters for Average scoring, 3 for Top-2.

studies.raters: 3 MTurk laypeople per scoring system; about 2,091 unique responses from 80 participants
studies.method: G-study and D-study, fully crossed p x i x r
studies.required_raters: With 2 items, no number of raters from 1 to 10 reached .80. With 3 raters: at least 4 AUT items or at least 8 consequences items. Phi stayed below .80 for every design considered. Snapshot scoring never reached .80.
studies.notes: Too few items cannot be compensated by more raters when person-by-item variance is large. Large rater main effects indicate severity differences.

studies.raters: Study 1: N = 132, 3 raters. Study 2: N = 298, 4 raters, 88,256 ratings
studies.criterion: Correlation with full-data scores; Rasch reliability
studies.method: Many-facet Rasch model with simulated missingness
studies.required_raters: No headcount. Rater workload could be cut by about one third with similar scores.
studies.notes: Severity differences were significant in Study 2.

studies.method: Cognitive workload effects on rater disagreement
studies.notes: Disagreement increases with workload (be-creative instructions; snapshot or complex response sets), implying that rater needs depend on scoring format.
Exact D-study coefficients were not retrieved.

studies.method: Spearman-Brown or resampling to smaller panels
studies.required_raters: No threshold established. 10 novices are insufficient, and even 106 novices converged poorly with experts.
studies.notes: Secondary sources disagree: Cseh and Jeffries give .53 for poetry; Kaufman et al. (2013) give .58 for poetry and .53 for stories.

studies.raters: 10 expert writers; quasi-expert subgroups of 9-12; 106 novices
studies.required_raters: 9-12 quasi-experts or 10 experts perform well; 10 novices do not.

studies.raters: 15 professional engineers; 31 first-year engineering students; 274 novices
studies.required_raters: No threshold established. Quasi-experts were not adequate substitutes for experts.
studies.notes: Only 5 products, so alpha rests on a very small sample of objects.

studies.required_raters: 10-15 for creativity ratings; about 15-20 for composite originality-practicality indices (product or Euclidean distance)
studies.notes: Individual raters were unstable over time.

studies.task: 90 Instagram fashion outfits, rated twice 2 or 4 weeks apart
studies.method: ICCs for the full panel and random panels of 3, 5, 7 and 10 raters
studies.required_raters: 7 or more for consistently exceeding .70, inter-rater and test-retest. 3-rater samples already exceeded .70 for test-retest, but not consistently.
studies.notes: Panel-specific ICC values were not retrieved.

studies.raters: Psychologists, art teachers, artists; panels of 3-21

studies.required_raters: Exact D-study numbers not verified. Dependability was low for all rater groups; van Hooijdonk et al. (2022) summarize that too many raters would be required for relative and absolute decisions.
studies.notes: Low dependability attributed to inconsistent rating procedure, scale use and beliefs about creativity. Rater inconsistency differed across tasks.

studies.task: 1 science and 1 social task; 137 primary pupils

studies.criterion: Expected reliability >= .80, framed through factor determinacy
studies.method: Simulation-based planned-missing design with GPCM, following Forthmann, Goecke and Beaty (2023)
studies.required_raters: 40 raters, 4 ratings per response for 50% of responses
studies.notes: A design solution for a specific rater budget and response pool, not a minimum for the domain.

studies.task: Individual compositions and group performances by pre-service teachers
studies.method: Reliability analysis with partial G-theory decomposition
studies.required_raters: No optimal number. Number of raters mattered far more than number of occasions.

studies.raters: Composers, music teachers, music theorists, seventh-graders, second-graders
studies.notes: Expert status alone did not guarantee consensus.

studies.task: Originality of creative decision making in soccer
studies.required_raters: Not tested. Part of a convention of about 3 raters.
studies.notes: Other Memmert-group game-test work reportedly used 3 trained experts on 1-10 scales (one consistency coefficient of .74). A goal-sequence study reportedly obtained .89-.92 with 3 UEFA A/Pro raters, known only from a practitioner summary. Neither has a confirmed citation here; locate the originals before citing.

studies.task: Review of 84 empirical studies of subjective creativity assessment
studies.raters: Most reviewed studies had fewer than 10 raters; mean and median about 5
studies.notes: Alpha differed through an interaction of domain and judge expertise.

studies.verification_note: As cited in Cseh and Jeffries (2019).

analytic_approaches.name: Spearman-Brown or alpha projection
analytic_approaches.procedure: Project single-rater reliability to k raters.

analytic_approaches.name: Resampling raters from a large pool
analytic_approaches.procedure: Draw repeated panels of size k; examine the distribution of reliability and convergence with full-panel or expert scores.
strengths: Shows risk across panels, not only the mean

analytic_approaches.name: Generalizability theory with D-studies
analytic_approaches.procedure: Decompose variance into person, rater, item and interaction components; project relative and absolute coefficients across rater and task numbers.
weaknesses: Does not scale or correct individual raters

analytic_approaches.name: Many-facet Rasch modeling
analytic_approaches.procedure: Estimate rater severity and fit; compute severity-adjusted scores; link raters through incomplete designs.
strengths: Corrects severity rather than only quantifying it

analytic_approaches.name: Judge response theory / IRT
analytic_approaches.procedure: Treat judges as items in GRM or GPCM models, yielding judge-specific discrimination and thresholds and reliability conditional on creativity level.
weaknesses: Needs adequate data for judge parameters
analytic_approaches.notes: Estimates of creativity levels are reported to be especially affected when judges are few.

analytic_approaches.name: Simulation-based planned-missing designs
analytic_approaches.procedure: Estimate parameters from prior or pilot data; simulate designs varying raters, ratings per response and share of doubly rated responses; evaluate against reliability and cost.
weaknesses: Depends on how representative pilot parameters are

limits_of_reliability_evidence.content: High consensus need not reflect domain creativity: 106 novices reached alpha = .94 on poetry yet correlated .22 with experts.
Do not affect alpha or relative G in fully crossed designs, but confound scores when raters score different subsets, and matter for phi.
Treated as error in classical and G-theory indices; JRT can partly model it as information.
In the same music data, individual creativity had alpha .90 but agreement .79.
Individual raters drift even when aggregates remain stable.

gaps_and_inconsistencies.inconsistent_targets: Alpha > .70, G or phi >= .80, generalizability >= .70, test-retest ICC >= .70, and factor determinacy >= .80 are not directly comparable.
gaps_and_inconsistencies.inconsistent_object_of_measurement: Person-level studies across tasks have tasks competing with raters; product-level studies have raters as the only facet.
secondary_source_discrepancies: Ten-novice poetry alpha is given as .53 or .58 depending on the citing paper.

planning_recommendations.note: Derived from this review; these are not published standards. The numeric fallback is a judgment call without direct empirical support.
steps: Define the object of measurement and decision type. Use relative G for correlational research; use phi or ICC(A) for absolute standards or rater-subset designs.

Run a pilot G-study with more raters than planned (e.g., 8-10 domain-matched raters, such as UEFA-licensed coaches for soccer, plus a quasi-expert group). Run D-studies over raters and situations, targeting >= .80 relative and reporting phi. Expect tasks or situations to be the bottleneck.
Resample the pilot panel (all k-subsets or about 1,000 draws) and report the distribution of reliability and full-panel correlation for k = 2 to 10.
Fit an MFRM or JRT model to quantify severity and judge discrimination and to flag misfitting raters. If rater load is high, simulate a linked planned-missing design.
Test rater-type validity by correlating quasi-expert or novice panels with experts, and collect discriminant ratings such as technical execution or effectiveness.
planning_recommendations.fallback_without_pilot: At least 5-7 domain experts for product ratings. Three raters only for short, homogeneous responses with trained raters and a clear rubric. Avoid fewer than about 10 lay raters for expert-domain products.
